thread.title: Big Tech Set Headaches With Exits of U.S. Cybersecurity Experts

author: Barron's
title: Big Tech Set Headaches With Exits of U.S. Cybersecurity Experts
text:
Getty Images/iStockphoto The View From Silicon Valley
The departures of a handful of cybersecurity officials from the Federal Bureau of Investigation less than four months before midterm elections has further complicated what is already a growing headache for some of tech's biggest players.
At least five officials have exited over clashes with the Trump Administration amid mounting concerns of cyber intrusions from Russia and other countries leading up to the Nov. 6 elections. The departures include: Scott Smith , an assistant FBI director in charge of the cyber division; David Resch , executive director of the FBI's criminal, cyber, response, and services branch; and Carl Ghattas , executive assistant director of the FBI's national security branch. The Wall Street Journal first reported the news , which was confirmed by the FBI.
Tech companies are under the gun to address voter meddling. Eight tech companies- Facebook ( FB ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon.com ( AMZN ), Alphabet 's Google ( GOOGL ), Twitter ( TWTR ), Snap (SNAP), and Verizon Communications (VZ) unit Oath -met with officials from the Department of Homeland Security and FBI at Facebook on May 23 to discuss the matter.
The meeting, initiated by Facebook, offered little solace-or information-to tech companies on specific threats they face, according to a representative from one of the companies in attendance. This person was not authorized to speak on the record.
Facebook and Twitter, heavily criticized for their unwitting roles in the 2016 presidential election, face the greatest threat: Further manipulation of their far-reaching social-media platforms through fake personae to shape debate and false or misleading news stories designed to help or hurt candidates.
Twitter took a significant step last week, with the purging of millions of fake or suspicious accounts as part of a larger cleanup effort. But, as it warned in a Q1 shareholders' letter, the elimination of the accounts had short-term consequences-its stock was hammered-and it is likely to report lower monthly active users (MAUs) during its second-quarter results on July 27.
At the same time, Facebook and Twitter took steps in late June to bring more transparency to ads leading into elections in the U.S. and elsewhere this year after Russian trolls were able to buy ads targeting U.S. voters in the months leading up to the 2016 presidential election.
The market's reaction to Twitter's bot purge underscores a lingering concern for tech companies with large platforms and audiences.
"Companies, especially in social media, are inherently conflicted," Edward Roberts , senior director of product marketing at Distil Networks, tells Barron's . "If they exhume all the bad actors, they risk driving down membership numbers and, ultimately, compromising their stock and market valuation."
Meanwhile, antiquated voting technology is in the crosshairs of hackers from Russia and, perhaps, other countries, intelligence officials from the DHS and FBI warned in April. To that end, Congress this year allocated $380 million to states to shore up those technologies and perform more post-election audits.
They are mindful of what happened in the last major election, when the DHS told 21 unidentified states that Russian operatives scanned their election systems for security holes in the months leading up to the 2016 U.S. presidential election.
In 2016, the threat was primarily from foreign countries. This year, it comes from them and supporters of both major American political parties, says Rodney Joffe , a senior vice president at data-analytics company Neustar .
